license.payload: Per item, recorded in origin.items. Nicolaus Copernicus died in 1543. The 1543 Petreius printing is in the public domain everywhere; the Internet Archive copy (Boston Public Library) carries no rights statement. The Commentariolus, unprinted in the author's lifetime, is seated from Leopold Prowe, Nicolaus Coppernicus, Bd. II (Berlin: Weidmann, 1884), public domain in the United States (published before 1931) and Prowe's own term long run (died 1887); the Google scan carries Google's usage request for non-commercial use, a request and no licence, recorded here. The Latin Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA 4.0 for the site's contributions, redistributed under the same licence.

normalization: Originals as fetched under original/: the Internet Archive scans with their OCR layers, and the Wikisource HTML as served with its revision ids. text/<slug>.ocr.txt is the Archive's OCR with line endings normalized; text/de-revolutionibus-ws.txt is the Wikisource parser output reduced by code, its eleven pages joined under '=== <title> ===' headings. No text was corrected by hand. The early-modern OCR is poor (long s read as f, ligatures broken); the loci in the OCR layers are phrases the OCR read correctly, and the canonical sentences are verified in the Wikisource layer.
scope: Held: De revolutionibus in its first printing (Nuremberg, 1543), the scan with its OCR layer, beside the Latin Wikisource transcription of the same printing (books I–VI with the front matter; the later books on Wikisource are themselves partly uncorrected OCR, kept as served). The Commentariolus, which circulated in manuscript and was first printed by Maximilian Curtze in the Mittheilungen des Coppernicus-Vereins 1 (Thorn, 1878), is held in Prowe's printing of 1884, the whole volume of Urkunden, pp. 184–202. Not held: the Curtze printing of 1878 (the Archive item mittheilungende00curtgoog, dated 1878, has an OCR layer of 35 KB in which the Commentariolus does not appear); the Narratio prima of Rheticus (1540), the Basel (1566) and Amsterdam (1617) editions, and the Letter against Werner. No modern edition is held.

why_seated: De revolutionibus is the book in which the Earth was set moving around the Sun, printed under a preface by another hand that called its hypotheses no more than devices for calculation. The seat holds the printing and its transcription side by side, so that the voice of Osiander and the voice of Copernicus can each be found at its own address. The Commentariolus is the first statement of the system, decades before the book.
